fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The System That Took the Land", "body": "Dylan Saccoccio tells Chance Garton that the impetus for his work is proving a system exists that quietly deprives people of property. He walks through Frank Almoin, the tenure by which monks held land while everything ultimately belonged to the pope under the papal bulls, then stacks the tithe laws, Ethelwulf in 855 making the whole English kingdom liable to tenths, King Guntham passing a similar law in 586, and Thomas Monroe finding that same ten percent land tax among the rajas of Ceylon, Travancore and Cochin. His blunt test is to stop paying property taxes on land you already own and watch what happens."}, {"title": "Sanskrit as the Script of the Sun", "body": "Dylan's method is philological, and he runs it live. He argues Sanskrit is scriptus sanctum, the holy writ or script of the sun, and that san, sean and shan carry the sun through Celtic, Nepali, Hindi and Italian alike. He traces shanakas, a judge of the feudal system, back through Godfrey Higgins to shanak and senate, and reads sockage from the root soc, which Blackstone glosses as liberty or privilege. Liberty, he insists, is not freedom. Chance Garton pushes on how the shush and s sounds slide between dialects, and why Hebrew needed a vowel point system at all."}, {"title": "Phoenicians Under Everything", "body": "The book's core claim is that the Phoenicians are the older layer beneath the classical world. Dylan says the Etruscans came out of the Phoenicians, that Italy was their primary colony, and that Britain and Ireland were peopled from there, which is why Irish carries Phoenician idioms. He inverts the standard family tree, arguing Latin descended from neither Greek nor Sanskrit, and that Hebrew and Arabic took their letters from Phoenician without being kin to it. Reading O'Reilly's Irish Dictionary, he ties shankus to the Fenians, and reads Britannia not as land of tin but as the covenant of Tinia."}, {"title": "Pirates Against Pirates", "body": "Chance Garton frames the whole conversation as pirates hijacking pirates, and Dylan agrees that the priest class simply changes costume across centuries. He credits Michael Osarion for the Greek piratis, the ones with fire, and explains he named the book The Holy Sailors because these men had use of the letters, and the letters are what made them holy. The modern version, he argues, is corporate feudalism with BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street at the top, two of them carrying ships in their logos. Priest lines were families, both men note, which is why Cohen simply means priest."}, {"title": "Why the Disney Version Fails", "body": "Chance Garton says most people's mythology is the Disney version, Hercules as a cartoon and Thor as a Marvel character, and that most of what was written after 1850 is really the Disney of its own era, including some of George Washington Carey's work. Both men insist they are not trying to take anyone's religion away, only to show the older and more rigid system underneath it. Dylan quotes Robert Taylor saying Christianity and paganism differ about as much as six and half a dozen, and closes by suggesting the night sky was once a memory palace anyone could fill."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Dylan Saccoccio joins Chance to discuss his book The Holy Sailors, the latest installment in the Spirit World series. The conversation focuses on the origins of feudalism, monasticism, and the priest-class systems that have shaped how land, law, and power have operated for centuries, and the linguistic and historical evidence that points to a common Phoenician root underneath all of it.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In this session: why "holy" in Holy Sailors refers to those who possessed the letters and could shape laws and religions at will, the dating problems with the Targums of Jerusalem, why ecclesiastical terms like diocese, dean, cardinal, and bishop are originally law and judiciary words rather than spiritual ones, the feudal template of all land belonging to the conqueror, the universal 10% tithe appearing across unconnected cultures, Webster's 1828 definition of "purchase" as conquer and rob, the lex non-scripta system of land transfer before the deed, Dylan Son of the Sea as the Welsh Noah, the Kabiri and the Phoenician Trinity, and why Britannia encodes the Covenant of Tina.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "One Sun God Behind a Dozen Names", "body": "Deep in the members-only stretch, Dylan traces a single solar deity across a dozen disguises: the Celtic Tutatis, the Egyptian Thoth or Teutus, the Phoenician Bel and Magon, and Jesus himself, whom he equates with Mars through the Syrian name Haziz. He cites Julian the Apostate's oration of the sun quoting Phoenician theology directly, and walks through Anubis Latrans worshipped in Britain as a hidden dog god tied to secret pontifical decrees. The throughline is that every culture's chief god turns out to be the same solar figure wearing a different regional mask, passed along Phoenician trade routes."}, {"title": "Britain's Five Languages and a Hidden Fleet", "body": "Dylan lays out the five historic languages of Britain, English, the British tongue of Wales, Cornish and Devonshire speech, the language of the Orkney Isles, and a gothic or Danish strain tied to Norway, arguing each layer marks a different wave of the same seafaring culture. He ties ancient Italians, Venetians, Britons and Scandinavians together as descendants of one maritime empire that spread language, temple building and religious symbolism along trade routes, noting the Norse specifically raided only in spring and summer because their ships and gear couldn't survive open winter seas."}, {"title": "Brutus of Troy and the Zodiac in Disguise", "body": "Dylan retells the myth that Britain was founded by Brutus of Troy, grandson of Aeneas, who supposedly assassinated his uncle, the seventh and last king of Rome. He reframes the whole story as disguised sky lore: the uncle's death marks the sun's summer turn, when the constellations visible at night are blotted out by daylight and effectively die. Rather than real history, he calls this pattern asteroid theology, arguing that historians who treat these kinglists as literal chronicles, without recognizing the embedded zodiac, end up building shoddy history on top of what was actually astronomical allegory."}, {"title": "Doubts About the Rosetta Stone", "body": "Dylan raises a specific, provable suspicion: no ancient or contemporary historian ever mentions the Rosetta Stones, despite there being three of them, and the earliest documented reference to related scripts like cuneiform traces only to the 1700s. His conclusion is a stark either or: either hieroglyphs are a modern invention, or the Rosetta Stones themselves are fakes that nobody can actually read, planted so a discoverer could claim credit for cracking a code that was manufactured rather than deciphered."}, {"title": "Coins, Pliny and a King Before Rome", "body": "As proof rather than speculation, Dylan points to coins of Cunobelinus, a king documented in pre-Roman Britain whose name folds together cuno, meaning born or begotten, and Bel, the Phoenician lord god, making him literally the son of Bel. He pairs that with Pliny's observation that druids used Greek characters identical to those Caesar era Greeks used, evidence he says ties the druidic system straight back to Phoenician and Egyptian originals. He closes the block by explaining his own rule: he only prints what he can source and hand to readers to verify, because he wants people equipped, not simply told, what to believe."}]
